title: Recursion
tagline: A function that calls itself — elegant, dangerous, and essential for trees, graphs, and divide-and-conquer algorithms.

sections.content:
There is a joke among programmers: *to understand recursion, you must first understand recursion*. It sounds like a riddle, but it captures something real — recursion is one of those ideas that initially feels circular, almost paradoxical, until the moment it clicks. Then you cannot stop seeing it everywhere: in file systems, compilers, sorting algorithms, game trees, mathematical proofs, and the structure of human language itself.

**Recursion** is when a function calls itself as part of solving its own problem. The trick is that each self-call works on a *strictly smaller* or *simpler* version of the original problem. Eventually the problem shrinks to something so trivial it can be answered directly — the **base case** — and from there the answers propagate back up through every pending call like a chain of dominoes falling in reverse.

This might sound like sleight of hand. How can a function that calls itself ever terminate? The answer is the same reason a shrinking Russian nesting doll eventually has nothing left inside it: the input must get smaller with every call, and the base case catches the bottom. Without those two guarantees — strict shrinkage, reachable base case — you have not written recursion, you have written an infinite loop that will crash the program.

Why does recursion matter beyond novelty? Because many of the most important data structures and algorithms are *inherently recursive*. Binary trees have a recursive definition: a tree is either empty, or it is a node with a left subtree and a right subtree — both of which are trees. Parsing expressions like `2 * (3 + 4)` is recursive because sub-expressions can nest arbitrarily deep. Merge sort works by recursively dividing an array in half, sorting each half, and merging the results. Recursion is not a trick for clever code golf; it is the natural language for problems that are self-similar at different scales. This chapter will build a complete, precise mental model: the mechanics of the call stack, the two mandatory components of every recursive function, why naive recursion can be exponentially slow, and how to fix that with memoization and dynamic programming.

sections.caption: Every recursive function has two phases: the descent (decomposing into smaller sub-problems) and the unwind (combining results back up). The base case is the turning point between the two.

sections.title: Russian Nesting Dolls and the Open Doll Stack
sections.content:
Imagine a set of Matryoshka (Russian nesting) dolls. To find the smallest doll inside, you open the outermost one and look inside. If there is another doll, you open that too and set the outer doll's halves on the table. You keep going — open, set aside, look inside — until you find a doll with nothing inside. That is the **base case**. You announce 'found the smallest!' and then work backwards: close the last pair you opened, close the one before that, all the way back to the original outer doll.

Each 'opening' maps to a **recursive call**. Each 'handing back the answer' maps to a **return value**. The pile of open doll halves on the table is the **call stack** — one pair per call currently in flight. If the dolls were infinitely nested, the pile would eventually topple off the table. That is a **stack overflow**: the call stack exhausts its memory limit and the runtime crashes.

This analogy also captures why the call order matters: you cannot close a doll until you know whether what's inside it is the smallest. Similarly, a recursive call cannot finish until its inner calls finish. All pending calls must wait, occupying stack space, until the base case is reached and results start flowing back. The stack is not just an implementation detail — it is the essence of how recursion's deferred computation works.

sections.title: The Two Mandatory Components of Every Recursive Function
sections.content:
Every correctly written recursive function has exactly two parts, and both must be present and correct:

**1. The base case** is the condition that stops the recursion. It handles the simplest possible input — the one you can answer directly without any further recursive calls. For `factorial`, the base case is `n <= 1`: we know `factorial(1) = 1` and `factorial(0) = 1` by definition, no further calls needed. For tree traversal, the base case is a null node: if the node does not exist, the subtree sum is zero. For binary search, the base case is when the search interval is empty.

If the base case is missing or unreachable, the function recurses forever. The stack grows without bound until the runtime throws a stack overflow error (in JavaScript: `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`).

**2. The recursive case** handles any input that is not the base case. It must do two things: (a) call the function with an input that is strictly closer to the base case — smaller number, shorter list, fewer nodes — and (b) use the result of that recursive call to compute and return an answer. The key word is *strictly*: if your recursive call uses the same input, you have an infinite loop. If it uses a larger input, you have an infinite loop that grows faster.

A clean way to think about the recursive case is the **leap of faith**: *assume the recursive call correctly solves the smaller sub-problem*. You do not need to mentally trace through the entire recursion — just trust the contract and write the logic to combine the smaller result into the larger one. This is the mental move that makes recursion feel natural once it clicks.

sections.title: The Call Stack: What Actually Happens in Memory
sections.content:
When a function is called, the runtime allocates a **stack frame** (also called an activation record) in the call stack. This frame holds: the function's local variables, the current value of its parameters, and the **return address** — the instruction to jump to when the function is done. Frames are arranged in a last-in-first-out (LIFO) stack: the most recently called function sits on top.

In a recursive function, each call creates a new, independent frame with its own copy of all local variables. When `factorial(4)` calls `factorial(3)`, a new frame is pushed. The frame for `factorial(4)` is *paused* — it is sitting on the stack, waiting — while the frame for `factorial(3)` runs. When `factorial(3)` eventually returns, its frame is *popped* and the frame for `factorial(4)` resumes from exactly where it left off, using the returned value to complete its own computation.

This is why recursion uses **O(n) stack space** for depth-n recursion: at maximum depth, all n frames are simultaneously alive on the stack. A recursive function over an array of 100,000 elements would push 100,000 frames — almost certainly causing a stack overflow, because stacks have a fixed memory limit (typically 1–8 MB depending on platform and browser).

**Call stack depth limits in practice**: In V8 (Node.js, Chrome), the call stack limit is roughly 10,000–15,000 frames depending on the function's frame size. In Firefox it is similar. In Python the default is just 1,000, deliberately conservative. You can check in Node.js with a quick test — `function f(n){ return f(n+1); } f(0)` — it will error around 15,000. For recursive algorithms over large inputs, this is a real engineering constraint.

**Unwinding and return values**: As frames pop off the stack during the unwind phase, each one's return value is passed back to the frame below it. The frame below resumes, uses that value in its own computation, and then returns *its* result to the frame below it. This cascading return is why the result 'comes back up' through the call chain.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The three examples illustrate the same two-part pattern: a base case that returns directly, and a recursive case that calls with a strictly smaller input. `countDown` prints before the recursive call, so numbers appear in descending order. If you move the print *after* the recursive call, they appear in ascending order — the print happens on the way back up. This before-vs-after distinction is the foundation of pre-order vs post-order tree traversal.

sections.title: Tree Traversal: Where Recursion Truly Shines
sections.content:
Binary trees are the canonical example of a **recursively defined** data structure. A binary tree node has a value and two children — left and right — each of which is either null (an empty tree) or another node (a smaller tree). The structure is self-similar at every level, and recursive code maps onto it with an almost uncanny directness.

There are three classic traversal orders, each differing only in *when* you visit the current node relative to its children:

- **Pre-order** (node → left → right): Visit the current node first. Useful for copying a tree or serializing it.
- **In-order** (left → node → right): Visit the current node *between* its children. For a binary search tree (BST), this visits nodes in sorted order — a property used in sorting algorithms.
- **Post-order** (left → right → node): Visit the current node last. Useful for deleting a tree (children must be deleted before their parent) or computing aggregate values that depend on sub-tree results.

Each traversal is a single recursive function. The only thing that changes is the line order. This elegance — three algorithms, all virtually identical except for placement of one statement — is only possible because the recursive structure of the code mirrors the recursive structure of the data.

For comparison, writing an iterative in-order traversal requires explicitly managing a stack data structure in your code. The recursive version uses the *call stack* as that stack automatically. Recursion is not magic; it is outsourcing stack management to the runtime.

The null check `if (!node) return 0` is the base case; it handles leaf children and completely empty trees uniformly.

sections.title: The Fibonacci Trap: When Naive Recursion Explodes
sections.content:
The Fibonacci sequence is defined recursively: `fib(0) = 0`, `fib(1) = 1`, `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)`. The recursive definition translates directly into code with almost no thought — which is exactly the trap.

The naive recursive implementation has **O(2^n) time complexity**. To see why, draw the call tree for `fib(5)`. `fib(5)` calls `fib(4)` and `fib(3)`. `fib(4)` calls `fib(3)` and `fib(2)`. `fib(3)` is computed twice! Go deeper and `fib(2)` is computed three times, `fib(1)` five times. The call tree is roughly a binary tree of depth n, so the total number of function calls is approximately 2^n.

For `fib(50)`, naive recursion makes roughly 2^50 ≈ 10^15 calls — more than a quadrillion. A modern CPU does around 10^9 simple operations per second, so this would take over a million seconds. For `fib(100)`, we are into cosmological timescales. The algorithm is *technically correct* but *practically useless* beyond small inputs.

This is not a flaw of recursion itself — it is a flaw of **redundant computation**. The fix is to remember results. Once you compute `fib(3)`, store it. Next time someone asks for `fib(3)`, return the cached value instantly. This technique is called **memoization** (note: *memo*-ization, from 'memo', not 'memory' — though the result is the same). With memoization, each unique sub-problem is computed exactly once, reducing time complexity from O(2^n) to O(n) — a dramatic, exponential-to-linear improvement.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["fib(5)"] --> B["fib(4)"]
  A --> C["fib(3)"]
  B --> D["fib(3)\nDUPLICATE"]
  B --> E["fib(2)"]
  C --> F["fib(2)\nDUPLICATE"]
  C --> G["fib(1)"]
  D --> H["fib(2)\nDUPLICATE"]
  D --> I["fib(1)"]
sections.caption: Naive Fibonacci recomputes the same sub-problems repeatedly. fib(3) is computed twice, fib(2) three times. With memoization, each node is computed once and cached — the duplicate branches are eliminated.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The memoized version passes a `Map` through every call. Before computing, it checks the cache. After computing, it stores the result. The bottom-up DP version eliminates recursion entirely by computing in the natural order (small to large) and keeping only the last two values. For production code over large inputs, bottom-up DP is preferred because it avoids stack growth. Memoization is preferred when the recursion structure is complex and not all sub-problems need to be solved (sparse recursion trees).

sections.title: Recursion vs. Iteration: Making the Right Choice
sections.content:
A foundational theorem in computer science states that **any recursive algorithm can be rewritten iteratively, and vice versa**. They are computationally equivalent — equally powerful. So when should you choose one over the other?

**Use recursion when:**
- The problem or data structure is inherently recursive (trees, graphs, nested structures, grammars).
- The recursive solution is dramatically clearer than the iterative one — compare a 5-line recursive tree traversal to the 20-line iterative version with an explicit stack.
- Input size is bounded and stack overflow is not a realistic risk.
- You are implementing a divide-and-conquer algorithm (merge sort, quicksort, binary search) where the recursive structure matches the algorithm's logic.

**Use iteration when:**
- You are processing flat, linear data structures (arrays, linked lists).
- Input size could be very large and stack overflow is a concern.
- Performance is critical — function call overhead (pushing/popping frames, argument passing) is measurable in tight loops.
- The iterative version is not significantly harder to understand.

**The performance reality**: In JavaScript, function calls are not free. Each call involves allocating a frame, passing arguments, saving/restoring registers, and jumping. For a simple sum over a million numbers, the iterative `for` loop is both faster and safer than recursion. Profiling data from V8 shows that recursive functions can be 2–5x slower than equivalent iterative code for flat-data problems, due purely to call overhead.

**When recursion is the only practical choice**: Some problems, like depth-first search of a graph of unknown depth, are so naturally expressed with recursion that writing an iterative version requires implementing your own explicit stack — which is essentially manually simulating what the call stack does automatically. At that point you have the worst of both worlds: iterative code with all the complexity of recursion but none of the clarity.

sections.title: Tail-Call Optimization: The Elegant Escape Hatch
sections.content:
A **tail call** occurs when a recursive call is the very last operation a function performs — its return value is immediately returned with no further computation. The function does nothing with the result except pass it along.

In `factorial(n) { return n * factorial(n-1); }`, the multiplication `n *` happens *after* the recursive call returns. The current frame must stay alive to perform that multiplication. This is **not** a tail call.

A tail-recursive factorial accumulates the result in a parameter: `function factTail(n, acc) { if (n<=1) return acc; return factTail(n-1, n*acc); }`. Here the call to `factTail(n-1, n*acc)` is the very last thing — no work remains after it. This **is** a tail call.

Why does this matter? A compiler or runtime that implements **tail-call optimization (TCO)** can recognise a tail call and *reuse the current frame* instead of pushing a new one. The existing frame's parameters are updated with the new arguments, and execution jumps back to the top of the function. The stack never grows — tail-recursive functions use **O(1) stack space** regardless of recursion depth.

With TCO, you get the expressive clarity of recursion without the stack overflow risk. The bad news: **V8 (Node.js and Chrome) does not implement TCO**. It is in the ES2015 specification, but Chrome engineers decided not to implement it, citing concerns about stack trace quality and tooling complexity. Safari's JavaScriptCore does implement it. So in Node.js, even a perfectly tail-recursive function pushes a new frame for every call — O(n) stack space, same as any other recursion. This is a deliberate trade-off, not an oversight, and it means that in JavaScript production code, deep recursion must be unrolled to iteration manually if input sizes are large.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Regular recursion\nn * factorial(n-1)"] --> B["Frame stays alive\nto do multiplication"]
  B --> C["Stack grows: O(n)"]
  D["Tail recursion\nreturn factTail(n-1, acc)"] --> E["Frame can be reused\nno pending work"]
  E --> F["With TCO: O(1) stack"]
  E --> G["V8 without TCO: O(n) stack"]
sections.caption: The distinction between tail and non-tail calls. TCO converts O(n) stack growth into O(1) by reusing frames. V8 does not implement TCO, so JavaScript tail calls still grow the stack.

sections.title: Common Recursion Patterns in Real Algorithms
sections.content:
Recursion powers a family of algorithmic strategies you will encounter throughout computer science:

**Divide and Conquer** splits a problem into independent sub-problems of the same type, solves each recursively, and combines the results. Merge sort divides an array into two halves, recursively sorts each, and merges the two sorted halves. Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions the array around it, and recursively sorts each partition. Binary search cuts the search space in half each time. All three have O(n log n) or O(log n) complexity arising from the logarithmic recursion depth.

**Backtracking** is the pattern for combinatorial search: try a choice, recurse into the consequences, and if you hit a dead end, undo the choice and try the next option. Solving a maze, generating all permutations, placing N queens on a chess board, and solving Sudoku are all backtracking problems. The recursive structure makes the 'try and undo' pattern clean: when the recursive call returns, you are back at the state before the choice, ready to try the next alternative.

**Depth-First Search (DFS)** on a graph explores as far as possible along a path before backtracking. The recursive implementation is essentially free: visit a node, mark it as visited, recursively visit each unvisited neighbor. The call stack implicitly maintains the path being explored. DFS is used for topological sorting, finding connected components, and cycle detection.

**Structural recursion** follows the recursive structure of data. JSON parsing, HTML/XML parsing, evaluating arithmetic expressions with parentheses, and interpreting programming languages all use structural recursion over a tree (the abstract syntax tree). Compilers are largely recursive programs that walk and transform these trees.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["mergeSort(arr)"] --> B["Split: left half"]
  A --> C["Split: right half"]
  B --> D["mergeSort(left)"]
  C --> E["mergeSort(right)"]
  D --> F["sorted left"]
  E --> G["sorted right"]
  F --> H["merge(sorted left, sorted right)"]
  G --> H
  H --> I["sorted arr"]
sections.caption: Merge sort is a canonical divide-and-conquer algorithm. The recursion tree has depth log₂(n), and each level does O(n) merge work, giving O(n log n) total. The recursive structure makes the algorithm's correctness argument simple: if the sub-arrays are correctly sorted, a linear merge produces a correctly sorted whole.

sections.content: **Historical context**: Recursion as a programming concept was introduced by LISP in 1958, designed by John McCarthy at MIT. LISP had no loops — recursion was the *only* iteration mechanism. Recursive definitions of functions correspond directly to mathematical induction, giving LISP programs formal provability properties. The Church-Turing thesis and lambda calculus — the theoretical foundations of computation — are built entirely on recursive function application. When you write a recursive function, you are working in a tradition that predates electronic computers.

**Interview and debugging checklist for recursion:**

(1) **Define the base case first**, before the recursive case. Ask: what is the smallest input I can handle directly? Is the base case reachable from every valid input?

(2) **Write the recursive case using the leap of faith**: assume your function correctly solves smaller inputs, then use that result.

(3) **Trace one level by hand** (not the full recursion). For `factorial(4)`, just verify that `4 * factorial(3)` is the right expression given that `factorial(3)` returns `6`.

(4) **Check for stack overflow risk**: estimate the maximum recursion depth. If it can reach thousands for realistic inputs, convert to iteration or add memoization.

(5) **Spot exponential blowup**: if your function makes two or more recursive calls per invocation and sub-problems overlap, you almost certainly need memoization. Draw two levels of the call tree — if you see the same call appearing twice, memoize.

(6) **A common bug**: forgetting to `return` the recursive call result. `function f(n) { if (n<=0) return 0; f(n-1); }` — the call is made but its result is silently discarded. The function returns `undefined` for all non-zero inputs.

items: Every recursive function needs a **base case** (solves the smallest input directly) and a **recursive case** (calls itself with a strictly smaller input and combines the result). Both must be correct for the function to terminate.

Each call pushes a new **stack frame** on the call stack. Recursion of depth n uses O(n) stack space simultaneously — very deep recursion (thousands of frames) causes a stack overflow (`RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` in V8).

Recursion is the natural choice for **inherently recursive problems**: tree traversal, graph DFS, parsing nested structures, and divide-and-conquer algorithms like merge sort. The code mirrors the problem's structure.

Naive recursion with overlapping sub-problems can be **exponentially slow** (e.g., Fibonacci at O(2^n)). Adding **memoization** — caching each sub-result the first time it is computed — reduces this to O(n), an exponential-to-linear speedup.

**Tail-call optimization (TCO)** allows tail-recursive functions to reuse the same stack frame, achieving O(1) stack space. It is in the ES2015 spec but **V8 does not implement it** — all recursion in Node.js/Chrome still grows the stack.

Any recursive algorithm can be rewritten iteratively (with an explicit stack if needed). Prefer recursion for clarity when the structure is hierarchical; prefer iteration for flat data or when stack overflow is a real risk.

The **divide-and-conquer** and **backtracking** patterns are built on recursion. Merge sort, quicksort, binary search, DFS, and all combinatorial search algorithms (permutations, N-queens, Sudoku) are recursive at their core.

quiz.question: What are the two mandatory components of every correctly written recursive function?
options: A loop and a return statement
A base case that terminates and a recursive case that shrinks the input
A helper function and a main function
A memoization cache and a stack check
quiz.explanation: Every recursive function needs a base case (handles the smallest input directly, no further call) and a recursive case (calls itself with a strictly smaller/simpler input). Without the base case recursion is infinite; without proper shrinkage the base case is never reached.

quiz.question: What happens to the call stack as a recursive function descends deeper through its calls?
options: Old frames are reused, so stack size stays constant
A new independent frame is pushed for each call, growing the stack
The stack is flushed and restarted before each recursive call
Frames are stored on the heap to avoid stack overflow
quiz.explanation: Each recursive call allocates a new stack frame with its own local variables and return address. Frames accumulate during descent; at maximum depth all n frames are simultaneously live on the stack, giving O(n) stack space usage.

quiz.question: What is the value of `factorial(5)` where `factorial(n) = n * factorial(n-1)` and `factorial(1) = 1`?
quiz.explanation: factorial(5) = 5 * 4 * 3 * 2 * 1 = 120. The call unwinds: factorial(1)=1, factorial(2)=2, factorial(3)=6, factorial(4)=24, factorial(5)=120.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of naive recursive Fibonacci `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)`?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
quiz.explanation: Each call spawns two more calls, forming a binary call tree of depth n. The total number of calls is approximately 2^n because sub-problems are recomputed repeatedly without caching. fib(3) alone is computed multiple times in fib(5).

quiz.question: How does memoization improve recursive Fibonacci from O(2^n) to O(n)?
options: It automatically converts recursion to a loop
It caches each sub-result the first time it is computed so later calls return instantly
It increases the call stack size limit to handle more frames
It reorders the recursive calls to avoid redundant computation
quiz.explanation: Memoization stores the result of each fib(k) after its first computation. Any subsequent call for the same k returns the cached value in O(1) instead of recomputing the entire sub-tree. Since there are only n distinct sub-problems (fib(0) through fib(n)), total work is O(n).

quiz.question: Which traversal order visits a binary tree node BETWEEN its left and right children?
options: Pre-order (node → left → right)
In-order (left → node → right)
Post-order (left → right → node)
Level-order (breadth-first)
quiz.explanation: In-order traversal visits the left subtree, then the current node, then the right subtree. For a binary search tree this produces nodes in sorted ascending order — a key property used in BST-based sorting.

quiz.question: What causes `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` in a JavaScript recursive function?
options: The function returns a value that is too large to store
The base case is never reached, so frames keep accumulating past the stack limit
The recursive case uses more heap memory than available
The function is defined inside another function
quiz.explanation: When the base case is missing or unreachable, each call pushes a frame and calls again forever. The call stack has a fixed size limit (around 10,000-15,000 frames in V8). When that limit is exceeded, the runtime throws this error — a stack overflow.

quiz.question: What is a tail call, and why does it matter for stack usage?
options: A call at the end of a file; it terminates the program cleanly
A recursive call that is the very last operation, enabling runtimes to reuse the current frame instead of pushing a new one
A call that passes the result to a callback instead of returning it
A call that happens after the base case is detected
quiz.explanation: A tail call is one where the function's return value is the recursive call's return value with no additional computation. A runtime implementing TCO can reuse (overwrite) the existing stack frame rather than push a new one, keeping stack usage at O(1) regardless of recursion depth.

quiz.question: Does V8 (Node.js / Chrome) implement tail-call optimization as specified in ES2015?
options: Yes — tail-recursive functions use O(1) stack space in all modern Node.js versions
No — V8 deliberately does not implement TCO; tail calls still push new frames and the stack grows
Yes, but only when running in strict mode with the 'use strict' directive
Only for async generator functions using yield
quiz.explanation: TCO is part of the ES2015 specification but V8 does not implement it. Chrome engineers decided against it citing concerns about stack trace quality and debugging tooling. Safari's JavaScriptCore does implement TCO. In Node.js, all recursive calls grow the stack regardless of tail call structure.

quiz.question: For which scenario is converting recursion to iteration MOST important?
options: Traversing a 10-node binary tree in a user interface
Computing factorial(7) in a utility function
Summing an array of 500,000 numbers that could overflow the call stack
Parsing a 3-level nested JSON object
quiz.explanation: Recursion over 500,000 elements would push 500,000 frames, far exceeding V8's ~15,000 frame limit and causing a stack overflow. Flat data over large inputs is exactly the case where iterative code is not just faster but necessary. The other scenarios involve small, bounded depth where recursion is safe.
